introduction: “They that have forsaken their country for the purpose of teaching Our Cause, these shall the Faithful Spirit strengthen.” From its first decades the Bahá’í community spread by people who moved: Persian merchants to India and Egypt, Americans to Europe, Asia and Africa. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s Tablets of the Divine Plan made it a programme, and he wrote that he longed to go himself, “even though on foot and in the utmost poverty”. Abraham’s departure, the disciples sent out without purse, the church “scattered abroad” and Ruth’s adoption of another people are the scriptural precedents. Kipling’s poem, from the same years, is a reminder of what else was travelling the world then, and of the question any people visited may fairly ask.
questions: Why do the readings attach such blessing to leaving home?
Ruth said, “thy people shall be my people”. How is that different from going abroad to change a people?
Reading 2 tells teachers to move on where teaching would cause trouble. What does that say about the manner of the enterprise?

outside.why: Believers should be sent to other regions. They that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Teachers must travel; where teaching would cause mischief, let them go elsewhere. Whosoever shall not receive you, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet.
Be mindful of the travellers and emigrants. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Emigrate to other lands for the sake of God’s Cause. Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house.
In movements there is blessing. He that observeth the wind shall not sow.
O that I could travel, even on foot and in poverty. In journeyings often, in weariness and painfulness, in hunger and thirst.
Teachers must continually travel to all parts of the continent. Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes.
The reading cites this text: go ye therefore, and teach all nations.
O Divine Herald! How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace.
Blessed art thou for having detached thyself from thy home. Lo, we have left all, and have followed thee.
Thou who hast migrated unto God. He went out, not knowing whither he went.
Those who have forsaken their country. Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
The most meritorious service is to bring the light. How shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?

Movement from place to place for the sake of God has always had its influence. The readings’ own decades sent others abroad with a different confidence: take up the White Man’s burden, send forth the best ye breed. What distinguishes the traveller the readings bless from the missionary of empire, and how would the people visited know?
